questions.q: Why is committing a large dataset directly into a Git repository usually a bad idea?
options: Git cannot store binary files at all
Git keeps every version of every tracked file forever, so the repository balloons, clones slow down, and binary diffs are meaningless
Git automatically deletes files larger than 1MB
Datasets must be stored as plain text to be versioned
questions.explain: Git's full-history model works well for text but poorly for large, frequently-changing binary datasets, bloating the repository without providing meaningful diffs.

questions.q: What does a `.dvc` file actually contain?
options: A full copy of the dataset, compressed
A small pointer containing a content hash (and metadata like size) that DVC resolves to the real data in remote storage
The Python code used to train the model
A list of all Git commits that touched the dataset
questions.explain: The .dvc file is a tiny, Git-trackable pointer — the actual data bytes live in a configured DVC remote like S3, addressed by that hash.

questions.q: What does `dvc repro` do differently from simply re-running every stage in a dvc.yaml pipeline from scratch?
options: It only re-runs stages whose declared dependencies have actually changed, reusing cached outputs for the rest
It deletes all previous outputs before running anything
It only works on the first stage of the pipeline
It ignores the dvc.yaml file entirely and re-trains from raw data every time
questions.explain: dvc repro is dependency-aware, similar to a build tool like Make — it skips stages whose inputs haven't changed and reuses their cached outputs.

questions.q: What problem does lakeFS solve that a plain DVC-per-file approach does not handle as naturally?
options: Running Python training scripts faster
Providing Git-like branching and commits over an entire data lake bucket, suited to multiple people experimenting against overlapping data concurrently
Storing model weights instead of data
Automatically labeling training data
questions.explain: lakeFS operates at the scale of a whole data lake, giving branch/merge semantics across the entire bucket rather than versioning individual files.

questions.q: How does Delta Lake provide data versioning without a separate tool like DVC?
options: By storing every table as a pickle file
By adding a transaction log on top of Parquet files, giving every table built-in time travel such as VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF
By requiring a Git repository for every table
Delta Lake does not support data versioning
questions.explain: Delta Lake's transaction log tracks every change to a table, enabling time travel queries directly against the table without any additional versioning tool.
